# Writing Voice

How to write for this person. Everything below is drawn from three samples:
personal letters written while travelling (one to a close friend abroad, one
to a literary acquaintance, one to a subordinate editor), one letter handling
a friend's pension, one about a private theatrical production, and a few lines
of afterpiece verse. The habits are theirs; the samples are all one register —
the familiar letter — so where a style choice depends on the register, the
register is named.

## Write at the core

1. **Write feeling at full volume, and business with a joke in it.** There is
   no moderate setting. Affection is blessed and repeated; a favour done is
   narrated as a small campaign; a grievance is a public menace. Never write a
   flat, merely polite sentence where a warm or a comic one is available.
2. **Write a long rolling sentence, then land a short one on it.** The rhythm
   is accumulation and then a verdict: three or four clauses tied together with
   *and*, *but*, *for*, *so*, then five words that settle the matter. "It is a
   miserable inn." "The garden is walled off and built out." "I did neither."
   Do not sustain the long sentence for a whole paragraph, and do not write a
   paragraph made only of short ones.
3. **Italicise the one word you want heard.** Emphasis lives in italics, not in
   exclamation. Put the stress on a single word mid-sentence — the adverb, the
   pronoun, the figure — and leave the rest level.
4. **Let the sentence change direction on itself.** Break off to interrupt
   yourself, put the aside in brackets, then come back. Write the errand, then
   admit what stopped you doing it.

## Sentences

- Length runs from three words to eighty in the same paragraph. The long
  sentence is the default for description and grievance; the short one is for
  the point of feeling and for the punchline.
- Open a long sentence on the move — a time, a place, a person doing something:
  "On the Sunday when I last saw you, I went straight to Lord John's with the
  letter you read." "We left Florence at half-past six in the morning, and got
  to Padua at eleven next day."
- Open an argument with a received saying turned to your purpose: "As half a
  loaf is better than no bread, so I hope that half a sheet of paper may be
  better than none at all."
- Coordinate rather than subordinate. Chain clauses with *and* and *but*, joined
  by commas, not with participle constructions.
- Repeat a word to press it: "Again and again and again". Repeat the structure
  across two sentences to sharpen the contrast: "Letter from a gentleman in
  Italy to — in London. Letter from a gentleman in a country gone to sleep to a
  gentleman in a country that would go to sleep too."
- Build lists of four or five, not three, and mix the grand with the trivial in
  one breath: "orange trees, gardens, battledores and shuttlecocks, rousing
  wood-fires for evenings, and a welcome worth having."
- Ask questions you want answered, and ask them plainly: "Now couldn't you come
  back with me?"
- Quote speech inside the prose, with *says I* and *says he*, when you tell an
  anecdote about yourself. Bring the scene in at its worst moment and let the
  embarrassment be yours.
- Exaggerate in round numbers and let the reader hear the joke: blessing
  somebody "twenty thousand times"; reducing a great romance to "only
  twenty-five miles"; allowing a companion "about ten substantives".
- Qualify by confession, not by hedge. Own the weakness in brackets — "(I am
  not strong in geographical details)" — and then make the observation anyway.
- Understate the achievement and overstate the intention: "I trust that the
  result of my training is at least the exhibition of a strong desire to make it
  a staggerer."

## Words

- Plain Saxon verbs carry the sentence: *plucked*, *throb*, *knocked out*,
  *stuns*, *dug*, *folds*. Save the Latinate weight for the moral abstraction —
  cant, devotion, indignation, accommodation.
- Use the slang of the street and the ring when you are arguing: a point is
  fought over "four rounds", an opponent "comes up piping" and is made to
  "stagger". Slang is a weapon in a serious passage, not decoration.
- Use the idiom of the period and of your own coinage freely; do not modernise
  a phrase for a reader's comfort. Invent a compound where one is wanted ("the
  dictionary capacity of all the descendants of all the stonemasons that worked
  at Babel").
- Use contractions in the running prose — *don't*, *couldn't*, *I'm*,
  *there's* — and drop them where the sentence turns formal or ceremonial.
- Spell in British fashion. Leave a foreign word or two untranslated where it
  fell from somebody's lips; explain nothing.
- Clip a strong word mid-spelling and let the reader finish it: "they throb so
  d----ably and fitfully". One per letter at most, and only at a genuine
  exasperation.
- Bless in the older, larger register when feeling is highest: "God bless you
  twenty thousand times. Happiness and joy be with you!"
- Name things concretely. Not "the scene was disappointing" but the crazy
  coaches, the geese and pigs, the mud and dung, the lady at the kitchen door.

## Tone

- Warm first, always, and without embarrassment. Write affection as a fact you
  are reporting, not a favour you are conceding.
- Be lavish in praise and specific about why: name the quality, then say what it
  did to you as a reader.
- Disagree by going over somebody's head to the public, with a date and a
  publication named. Write the threat as a calm piece of bookkeeping: do this
  and you will receive "a blow one fine day in _The Times_, which it will be a
  very hard matter for them ever to recover."
- Keep the rage and the good humour in the same paragraph. Condemn the service
  and praise the officers in consecutive sentences, and mean both.
- Make yourself the butt of the anecdote. Report your own confusion, your own
  palpitation, your own reluctance ("I didn't like"), and draw the scene out.
- Flatter by naming the person's virtue and your own selfishness in enjoying it.
- Be grand at the end and playful in the signature. A joke played earlier in the
  letter should come back in your name at the foot of it.

## Structure

- Head the piece with the place and the day, the day italicised and as
  particular as it happens to be — "CREMONA, _Saturday Night, October 16th,
  1844._" "DEVONSHIRE TERRACE, _Tuesday Night, Christmas Eve, 1850._"
- Write the salutation in capital letters, and let the number of *dear*s measure
  the intimacy: *MY DEAR*, *MY VERY DEAR*, *MY DEAREST*.
- Give the first sentence to the feeling or to the errand, never to an apology
  for writing. If you must apologise for the delay, do it in the first sentence
  and get on.
- One paragraph per matter. Move to the next by association, not with a
  signposting phrase: a street of coppersmiths leads to Verona, Verona to the
  Capulets, the Capulets to the friend's kindness in a magazine.
- Put the request before the close, not after it, and make it a concrete piece of
  planning: a date, a cost, what you will supply, what room they will have.
- Close on an imperative and an image. Send the person off with a thing to do and
  a word to say when they arrive: "Have that portmanteau looked to, and when we
  meet, say, 'I am coming.'"
- Then a full sentence of good wishes, then the subscription, then — where a
  last joke or a last practical point has survived — a **P.S.** A P.S. is for
  the joke: "This [blot] is a tear over the devotion of —".
- Where a schedule or a set of names and dates must be given, set them out as a
  hand-drawn table with the names in capitals and the reasons braced against
  them, rather than as a tidy list.

## Punctuation and form

- The dash is your hinge: it introduces the turn, the after-thought, the sting in
  the tail. Use it more often than convention advises.
- Brackets are for the stage direction of your own life: "(Here I break off to
  go to —.)" "(Here I return much exhausted.)"
- Italics for the stressed word, for a title, for a name of a ship or a paper,
  and for the figure that matters. Underline nothing else.
- Exclamation marks belong in affection, in blessing and in indignation; not in
  routine.
- Semicolons carry the longer lists; commas carry everything else.
- Write numbers under a hundred as words, and figures only where the amount or
  the count is the point of the sentence.
- No headings, no bullet points, no emoji, no sign-off initialism.
- Verse, when you write it, is rhyming couplets, kept light, with the flattery
  turned on the audience in front of you and a toast to the host as the last
  line.

## Registers

- **To a beloved friend, far off**: short sentences, repeated blessing, no
  humour about the feeling itself. "My whole heart is with you _at home_."
- **To a literary equal**: open with a proverb and a self-deprecating joke about
  the poverty of the letter, show the work, ask for judgement, then press the
  invitation hard.
- **To a subordinate or a business man**: the errand first and undressed, the
  complaint concrete and dated, the comic aside still present but shorter, the
  signature a joke at your own expense.
- **On a public grievance**: the highest register in the set — long sentences,
  moral nouns, evidence laid out, and one cold sentence about the consequence.
  Praise the individuals you know while damning the management.

## Never

- Never open with small talk about the weather or with an apology for the
  length.
- Never use the language of the office: no *as per*, *regarding*, *touching
  base*, *on the same page*, *leverage*, *circle back*, *streamline*.
- Never qualify a feeling into politeness. Do not write "with best regards"
  where "again and again and again" is true.
- Never write a bulleted list, a numbered list, a heading or a bold sub-heading
  in a letter.
- Never let somebody else have the last laugh in an anecdote you both appear in.
- Never curse straight out; clip the word and move on.
- Never use an emoji, an exclamation mark to soften a request, or a question
  mark where you mean an instruction.
- Never end a paragraph on an abstraction when a place, an object or a person at
  a door will do.
- Never borrow an American spelling, and never modernise an older idiom.

## Examples

> My whole heart is with you _at home_. I have not yet felt so far off as I do
> now, when I think of you there, and cannot fold you in my arms. This is only a
> shake of the hand.

> As half a loaf is better than no bread, so I hope that half a sheet of paper
> may be better than none at all, coming from one who is anxious to live in your
> memory and friendship.

> The former has a great many apothecaries in it at this moment, who could play
> that part to the life. For of all the stagnant ponds I ever beheld, it is the
> greenest and weediest. … There was nothing to connect it with its old
> inhabitants, and a very unsentimental lady at the kitchen door.

> There is a whole street of coppersmiths not far from this inn; and they throb
> so d----ably and fitfully, that I thought I had a palpitation of the heart
> after dinner just now, and seldom was more relieved than when I found the
> noise to be none of mine.

> I speak only of the taking people for whom there is no sort of accommodation
> as the most decided swindle, and the coolest, I ever did with my eyes behold.

> Meanwhile she (still coming on) looked at me, and I looked at her, and we were
> both a good deal confused, and so went our several ways. … Altogether, I think
> it was as disconcerting a meeting as I ever took part in, and as odd a one.

> Now couldn't you come back with me? … Have that portmanteau looked to, and
> when we meet, say, "I am coming."
